memories.memory: I have been married to Elaine for 38 years, and lately we have been arguing about whether to move closer to our daughter after retirement.
My son Daniel lives about four hours away, and I send him roughly $300 a month while he finishes an electrician apprenticeship, though I make a point of calling it a loan.
I am the deputy director of a regional public-works office, and I am quietly competing for the director position when my supervisor retires next spring.
Last November, I documented repeated missed deadlines by a program manager on my team, but senior leadership reassigned the work instead of approving the formal performance review I recommended.
I still have coffee with a former colleague, Marcus, every other Friday even though we left the department after disagreeing over how a major procurement was handled.
My younger sister has been helping our mother manage appointments and bills, and I feel guilty that my demanding work schedule leaves her carrying more of that responsibility than I do.
I turned down an early-retirement package worth about $42,000 because I want one more chance to lead the department through its five-year infrastructure plan.
